note: Virgil's. At the end of Canto 30 he scolded Dante sharply for listening to a quarrel, then comforted him.

context: His spear, which had been his father Peleus's, wounded the king Telephus, and the wound could be healed only by the spear itself. Poets before Dante had used it as an image for a lady's glance or kiss.
They leave the tenth and last ditch and cross the bank to the middle of the circle, where a great pit drops to the bottom of Hell.
The "holy company" is the band of knights who formed his rear guard, cut down at Roncesvalles in the Pyrenees as his army came home from Spain.
In the Song of Roland he blows his ivory horn so hard that his temples burst, and Charlemagne hears it many miles away, too late to save him.

note: Italian cities of Dante's time bristled with towers, built by the great families for defense and for show. In the dim light he takes the shapes ahead for another walled city, like the city of Dis that he entered in Inferno 9.

context: They stand in the pit with their feet on its floor, visible from the waist up above the rim.

note: The well at the center of Malebolge. Its floor, far below, is the ninth and last circle of Hell.
Monteriggioni, a fortress on a hilltop north of Siena, built by the Sienese in the early 1200s against Florence. Its ring of wall with fourteen towers is still standing.

context: Whenever it thunders, the giants are reminded of the thunderbolts that struck them down.

note: The Roman god of war. With no more giants born, war lost its most terrible soldiers.
Huge animals are no danger to mankind as a whole, because they have no reason. The giants had size and a mind as well.
A much-quoted warning: reason joined to ill will and to power is the most dangerous thing in the world. It applies to every sin of fraud and treachery in lower Hell, not only to giants.
An ancient Roman bronze pine cone, about thirteen feet tall. In Dante's time it stood in the forecourt of the old basilica of Saint Peter. It is now in a courtyard of the Vatican.
The people of Frisia, on the North Sea coast, were known for their height.
Gibberish. Scholars have tried to read it as garbled Hebrew or Arabic, but Virgil's words below settle the matter: it is a language no one else can understand.
The Bible calls Nimrod "a mighty hunter" (Genesis 10), so Dante gives him a hunting horn. It was the blast heard at the start of the canto.

context: The man who caused the confusion of tongues is left with a language of his own that no one shares, and can understand no one else's.

note: The Tower of Babel (Genesis 11). All people spoke one language until they tried to build a tower that would reach heaven. God confounded their speech so that they could not understand one another, and scattered them.
The usual direction of travel in Hell. They walk around the rim of the pit from one giant to the next.
A giant of Greek myth, son of Neptune. He and his twin brother Otus piled mountain on mountain to climb up to the gods, and were killed for it.

The battle of Phlegra, where the giants attacked Olympus and Jove destroyed them with thunderbolts. Dante reads it as the pagan counterpart of the Tower of Babel and of Lucifer's rebellion: pride reaching for heaven.

A giant of the war against the gods. In the Aeneid he has a hundred arms and fifty heads. Virgil here says he is shaped like Ephialtes, with an ordinary body, which many readers take as Dante quietly correcting his master's poem. Briareus is shown struck down in a carving in Purgatorio 12.

context: He was born after the giants' war on the gods and took no part in it. That is why he alone is unchained and can speak in human words.

note: The ninth circle, where traitors are punished. It is the floor of Hell and the center of the earth.
The valley of the river Bagradas, near Zama in what is now Tunisia. Lucan places the cave of Antaeus there. Virgil opens with flattery, in the high style of a formal request.

context: His victory at Zama was won in Antaeus's own country, which is why Virgil calls the valley blessed.

note: The Carthaginian general (247–about 183 BC) who invaded Italy and defeated the Romans at Cannae. Zama, in 202 BC, was his only great defeat, and it ended the war.
Lucan says Antaeus lived on the lions he caught.
Lucan again: he says Earth spared the gods by not sending Antaeus to fight at Phlegra. Virgil turns the poet's remark into a compliment.
The giants. In the myth they were born from Gaia, the Earth, and the word giant was explained as "earth-born".

Two more giants of myth. Tityos tried to rape the goddess Latona and was killed. In the underworld his body covers nine acres. Typhoeus, also called Typhon, fought Jove and was buried under Mount Etna. Virgil hints that he could always ask one of them.
Fame. Dante is alive and can speak of Antaeus when he returns to the world. The same offer has opened the mouths of many of the damned.
Unless God takes him to Heaven before his natural time. Dante was 35 and might expect to live to seventy. He died at 56.

context: He wrestled Antaeus and felt the strength of these hands before he found the way to beat him: holding him off the ground until his strength failed.
He wraps his arms around Dante so that the giant lifts the two of them as one.

note: The shorter of the two leaning towers in the middle of Bologna, built in the early 1100s and still standing. Seen from under its lean, with clouds moving the other way, the tower itself seems to be falling. Dante knew Bologna, and an early sonnet of his mentions the tower.

context: Named here before he is seen. He is at the very bottom, in the mouth of Lucifer (Inferno 34).
The first mention of what waits at the bottom of the pit.

note: The giant swings upright again like a mast being raised. Dante and Virgil now stand on the ice, far below his feet.
